newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Santa Fe approves merger with Newmont.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Santa Fe approves merger with Newmont.

text.p: Newmont Mining Corp. Monday won a three-month, $2.5 billion takeover battle for Santa Fe Pacific Gold Corp., which dropped a previous merger pact with Homestake Mining Co.
"The combination of Newmont and Santa Fe will create the largest gold company in North America," Newmont Chairman Ronald Cambre said in a statement.
The merged company will have 55 million ounces of proven and probable reserves and estimated gold production of 4 million ounces by 1998, Cambre said. Santa Fe has mines in Nevada and California.

"It's a very natural merger," said analyst Lawrence Glaser of brokerage Muzinich & Co. Glaser said the latest deal was part of a trend of mergers beginning in 1995 and influenced by lower gold prices, which make gold company stocks more affordable.

Under the agreement, Santa Fe stockholders will receive 0.43 of a share of Newmont common stock for each share of Santa Fe common stock they hold. Based on Newmont's closing price of $44.125 Friday, the transaction is valued at $18.97 for each Santa Fe share, or a total of $2.5 billion, the companies said.

Santa Fe said it paid Homestake a termination fee of $65 million, according to the terms of its prior merger pact with Homestake. "The $65 million probably will make a difference in earnings this year," Glaser said.
The deal also calls for five Santa Fe directors to join Newmont Mining's board, increasing its size to 15.
"Newmont turned this into a friendly deal by promising to put five extra directors on the board from Santa Fe," Glaser said.

With cash savings from the merger estimated at $70 million to $80 million a year, and predicted total cash costs in 1998 of about $210 for each ounce produced, Newmont said it expected to become one of the world's most profitable gold producers. On Monday, April gold added $3.20 to $352.70 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange.
Glaser said Homestake was expected to look for another company to acquire. "This week the market will be guessing what Homestake will go after," he said.
Monday's announcement marked a victory for Denver-based Newmont, which opened the struggle for Santa Fe Pacific Gold on Dec. 5 with a proposed stock swap valued at $2 billion.
Four days later, San Francisco-based Homestake proposed a stock swap merger valued at $2.3 billion. The deal was endorsed by the boards of both companies.
On Jan. 7, Newmont made its second play for Santa Fe, making an offer valued at $2.2 billion under which Santa Fe shareholders would receive 0.40 shares of Newmont stock for each Santa Fe share.
Albuquerque, N.M.-based Santa Fe agreed to open discussions with Newmont while keeping the agreement to merge with Homestake in effect.
Santa Fe Chairman Patrick James said in a statement that the company's board of directors met with Newmont and Homestake officials on Saturday and decided to go with Newmont's bid.
James said Newmont's bid was better, that Newmont would make a better fit with Santa Fe and that the deal offered "significant long-range potential for our shareholders."
He praised Homestake as an "outstanding company" and said its managers and board acted professionally during the merger talks.

"It was apparent that Homestake needed SFPG (Santa Fe Pacific Gold) more than Newmont," said analyst Marc Cohen of brokerage PaineWebber Group Inc., adding that Newmont was a better fit with Santa Fe.

Glaser estimated a merger with Homestake would only have saved $30 million to $40 million a year, as opposed to the $70 million to $80 million in annual cost savings predicted for the deal with Newmont.

The agreement is subject to approval by shareholders of both companies. The deal, which is expected to be tax-free to shareholders and to be accounted for as a pooling of interests, is expected to close during the second quarter.
Newmont stock dropped $1.125 to $43 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Santa Fe Pacific Gold stock rose 50 cents to $17.875 and Homestake Mining rose $1 to $16, also on the NYSE.
Homestake operates mines in California, South Dakota and British Columbia, and has interests in mines in Ontario and Australia.
